decisions.executionNote: Begin right-arm approach to the straightedge, gradually pitching the gripper down while preserving the starting elbow branch. Left arm stays at origin.
Continue gradual downward reorientation above the right end of the straightedge; keep clear of all three cubes.
Approach above the right portion of the tool while finishing the first stage of downward wrist pitch.
Bring the right gripper nearly vertical and above the tool, without descending into the tabletop.
Yaw the vertical gripper to close across the narrow width of the straightedge, adding a little clearance for the sweep.
Continue wrist yaw over the right-side workspace so the jaws will straddle the tool rather than its length.
Finish aligning the jaw opening normal to the tool and approach its right-hand section from above, using small offsets for visual correction.
Lower the open jaws toward the narrow straightedge, still away from the cubes. Visual depth and jaw centering remain uncertain.
The wrist view places the straightedge between the jaws. Stop descending and close around it at the observed contact height; do not lift any cube.
With the jaws closed on the tool, rotate it gently in the tabletop plane toward a horizontal pushing edge. Keep the tool low and the blocks on the table.
The tool did not visibly follow yaw, so retention is unconfirmed. Reopen and change to a slightly forward-tilted approach with the wrist farther back to gain depth and joint margin.
Recenter the open jaws around the visible tool and restore yaw matching its actual angle before another closure.
Use the tilted approach to seat the fingers slightly deeper around the straightedge, then close without lifting or approaching a cube.
Allow the gripper to finish closing at the observed height before testing whether the straightedge follows a planar motion.
Test planar retention by slowly swinging the straightedge toward horizontal, with no upward translation.
Advance the held/contacted straightedge slowly along the tabletop toward the blocks, checking its actual motion rather than assuming rigid retention.
The right-end push rotates the tool rather than translating it uniformly. Bring the left arm toward its left section for a two-point tabletop push, staying within each arm's workspace.
Continue the left approach with closed fingers to form a broad pushing contact behind the left part of the tool; keep the right contact stationary.
Position the left closed fingertips behind the left section of the straightedge at low height; right hand continues to steady the opposite section.
Push the left section forward while keeping the right endpoint steady, reducing the tool's diagonal angle before the coordinated push.
The left fingers passed above the tool. Back off and lower them gradually behind it to establish a real low pushing contact.
Back the left fingers away with clearance; their last motion was contact-limited and did not move the tool. Reapproach from the near side rather than forcing downward.
Lower the left closed fingertips on the near side of the straightedge, using the observed contact height and a small rearward margin.
Slide the left contact forward at its observed low height, aiming to move the left end of the straightedge while the right end is steadied.
Reposition the left fingertips farther behind the tool and pitch them more steeply down, avoiding the previous overpass of the narrow edge.
Advance the left low contact again with the steeper fingertip angle, watching for actual motion of the straightedge's left end.
Release the poorly constrained contacts and clear the left wrist. Let the straightedge settle before forming a better two-sided grasp; cubes remain untouched.
Reorient the left open gripper toward a top-down cross-width grasp of the tool, maintaining clearance and elbow continuity.
Continue rotating the left gripper so its jaws straddle the actual diagonal tool; keep the tool and cubes on the table.
Finish the left gripper's vertical cross-width alignment above the near end of the straightedge before descending.
Lower the aligned left jaws around a section just inside the tool's left endpoint, rather than pushing across its top.
Seat the left fingers a little lower around the tool and close both grippers. No cube is inside either jaw opening.
Hold both observed poses and allow the jaws to settle around the straightedge before attempting another planar alignment motion.
Use the now-straddling left grip to move the tool's left end forward in a shallow arc. Open the right jaws to avoid opposing the in-plane rotation.
The left end now follows the gripper. Continue its shallow forward arc to reduce the tool angle, keeping the same low height.
Continue straightening the tool while tilting the left wrist forward slightly to preserve joint margin. Compensate downward to keep the pushing edge on the tabletop.
The tool is now engaging the center cube. Bring its left end forward a little farther to make the pushing edge horizontal, with no lifting motion.
The straightedge is nearly horizontal and two cubes are seated against it. Close the right jaws at the existing contact before a short coordinated finishing push.
Apply a short coordinated forward push with both ends of the straightedge, tilting the wrists for reach margin while compensating vertically to keep the edge low.
All three cubes now appear parallel in a straight row. Release the straightedge without moving the arms so it can remain on the table before retreating to origin.
